questions.question: A netstat line reads '192.168.1.10:49152 -> 93.184.216.34:443'; each address-plus-port pair uniquely names one endpoint of the connection. What is that combination called?
questions.explanation: An IP address identifies the host and the port identifies the process; concatenating the two produces a socket, the unique endpoint a TCP connection binds to.

questions.question: A capture shows a polite four-packet close: the initiator's first packet carries one flag, answered by ACK; the peer then sends a packet with that same flag, answered by an ACK. Which flag initiates the teardown?
questions.explanation: The FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK sequence is the graceful four-way close; the flag each side sets to say 'I have no more data' is FIN - an RST would abort the connection instead.

questions.question: A receiver's buffer is nearly full, so it shrinks the value it advertises in a 16-bit TCP header field to slow the sender down. Which header field implements this receiver-side flow control?
questions.explanation: The receiver reports its remaining buffer space in the 16-bit Window field; shrinking it throttles how much unacknowledged data the sender may have in flight - that is TCP flow control (distinct from congestion control).

questions.question: During the TCP handshake, each host announces the largest payload it will accept per segment - typically 1460 bytes on Ethernet. What is this negotiated value called?
questions.explanation: The Maximum Segment Size option is exchanged in the SYN packets to declare the biggest data payload each side can receive in one segment, sized to avoid IP fragmentation.

questions.question: A ping test shows 1500-byte packets with the DF bit set fail across a tunnel while 1400-byte packets succeed. Which link-layer size limit is being exceeded?
questions.explanation: The largest packet a link can carry is its MTU; tunnel encapsulation shrinks the effective MTU below Ethernet's 1500, so oversized DF-marked packets fail rather than fragment.

questions.question: A 4000-byte IP datagram reaches a link that accepts only 1500-byte frames and exits as three packets sharing one identification field, all but the last carrying an offset and a 'more' indicator. Which process occurred?
questions.explanation: When a datagram exceeds the link MTU, routers split it into fragments that share the ID field and carry offsets plus a More-Fragments flag so the destination can reassemble them - a 4000-byte datagram needs three 1500-byte frames.

questions.question: An expected ACK for sent data never arrives; when the sender's timeout fires, it transmits the unacknowledged segment again. Which TCP reliability function is this?
questions.explanation: TCP tracks unacknowledged segments with a retransmission timer; when it expires (or after duplicate ACKs), resending the segment - classic ARQ-style error recovery - restores reliability.

questions.question: A firewall ACL must distinguish whether an IP payload is TCP (6), UDP (17), or ICMP (1) by reading one 8-bit IPv4 header field that identifies the encapsulated payload type. Which field is it?
questions.explanation: IPv4's 8-bit Protocol field numbers the next-layer payload (6=TCP, 17=UDP, 1=ICMP); IPv6 renamed the same function 'Next Header'.

questions.question: One public IP serves tens of thousands of simultaneous client sessions because each flow is kept distinct by its own source port number. Which technique makes this sharing possible?
questions.explanation: Because a session is identified by the full source IP:port / destination IP:port tuple, many flows can share one address; separating them by port number is port multiplexing (also the basis of PAT/NAPT).

questions.question: VoIP packets are queued for low latency while bulk backups are made to wait, enforced by packet marking and scheduling policies applied end to end. Which mechanism does this?
questions.explanation: Classifying, marking (e.g., DSCP), and scheduling traffic so delay-sensitive flows are served first is Quality of Service; FIFO forwarding alone could not differentiate the queues.

questions.question: A port scan hits a closed port and the host answers with a segment that kills the half-open attempt immediately - no graceful four-way close. Which flag was set in the reply?
questions.explanation: A segment with the RST (reset) bit aborts a connection outright - the standard response to a SYN aimed at a closed port - whereas FIN performs a graceful teardown.

questions.question: A daemon binds port 443, which requires elevated privilege, while a client picks 50000 from the dynamic range for its side of the connection. Within which range does the daemon's privileged port fall?
questions.explanation: Ports 0-1023 are the well-known/system range reserved for standard services and requiring privilege to bind; 1024-49151 are registered and 49152-65535 (where 50000 lives) are the dynamic/ephemeral range.

questions.question: On a 10 Gbps link with 100 ms RTT, the needed receive window exceeds the 16-bit field's 65,535-byte maximum, so a multiplier is negotiated inside the SYN packets. Which TCP option provides it?
questions.explanation: Keeping a fat, long pipe full needs windows larger than 64 KB; the Window Scale option, negotiated only during the handshake, left-shifts the advertised window by up to 14 bits.

questions.question: After three duplicate ACKs, a sender halves its sending rate - not because the receiver's buffer filled, but because the network itself dropped packets. Which TCP mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: The advertised window protects the receiver, but packet loss is treated as a sign the network is saturated; slow start/congestion-avoidance algorithms that shrink the congestion window are TCP congestion control.

questions.question: Working out MSS: Ethernet's 1500-byte MTU minus the 20-octet IPv4 header minus the minimum TCP header leaves 1460 bytes of payload. How many bytes is the TCP header without options?
questions.explanation: Rearranging 1500 - 20 - x = 1460 gives x = 20: the fixed TCP header is 20 bytes like IPv4's, and options can stretch it to a maximum of 60 bytes.

questions.question: A packet capture shows a host sending SYN, receiving SYN-ACK, and replying ACK to a web server. What process just completed?
questions.explanation: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK completes the three-way handshake, synchronizing sequence numbers and establishing the TCP connection.

questions.question: During a transfer the receiver advertises a TCP window size of 0. What must the sender do?
questions.answer: stop sending data until the window reopens
alternatives: wait for a nonzero window update
questions.explanation: A zero window means the receiver's buffer is full; the sender must pause and probe until the receiver advertises usable window space.

questions.question: A router discards an IP packet because its TTL reached 0. Which ICMP message is sent back to the source?
questions.explanation: When TTL hits zero the router drops the packet and returns ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11), the mechanism traceroute relies on.

questions.question: Ethernet has a 1500-byte MTU. With 20-byte IPv4 and 20-byte TCP headers, what is the maximum segment size (MSS) of TCP payload?
questions.explanation: MSS = MTU - IP header - TCP header = 1500 - 20 - 20 = 1460 bytes.

questions.question: The IPv4 Total Length field is 16 bits. What is the maximum theoretical size of a single IPv4 packet?
questions.explanation: A 16-bit length field can express at most 2^16 - 1 = 65,535 bytes, the theoretical IPv4 packet size limit.
